newsitem.title: FRANCE: Analysts unsure French bond gains can last.
newsitem.headline: Analysts unsure French bond gains can last.

text.p: French bond yields were trading at their lowest levels in decades on Monday but analysts were unsure the strong performance would last.
"We're still relatively concerned about how sustainable these gains are," said bond analyst Iain Lindsay of Credit Lyonnais. "The liquidity is relatively modest."
"I think the upside is very limited," he said.
Ten-year government bond (OAT) yields on Monday fell through the crucial psychological level of 5.50 percent and the March 10-year future was setting historic highs.

Building on Friday's gains, the yield on the 2006 OAT at 1430 GMT was 5.45 percent, its lowest level in 30 years, while the 10-year bond future broke through key resistance at 131.40. But volumes were extremely thin. The latest gains were triggered by the release of market-friendly U.S. data on Friday.

Some analysts said the outlook hinges on the direction of the U.S. market. "We're still under threat of some corrrection in the U.S. market," said Philippe Brossard of ABN Amro, who sees 10-year bond yields rising to 5.70 percent by March.
Others believe a supportive European interest rate climate could allow the French bond market to advance still further.

Last week's data showing the total number of jobless in Germany had hit 4.66 million people, "was extremely favourable to the European bond market," Nordine Naam of BIP said. BIP expects 10-year yields to fall to 5.30 percent by April.

"It (the data) makes one believe the interest rate climate will be accomodating on a sustainable basis," he said. He said more bad German economic news could mean more rate cuts by the Bundesbank, paving the way for easier French monetary policy.

Many analysts believe the Bank of France's five basis cut in its intervention rate to 3.10 percent on January 30 was its last unilateral cut. "If the Bundesbank eventually reduces its repo rate, the Banque de France could cut its intervention rate by the same magnitude," said Lindsay.
But he said the dollar's gains had given a monetary stimulus that may content French and German central banks for some time.
Other analysts said 5.50 percent was likely a peak in 10- year yield terms. "But it is true there's a buying story in the French market," said economist Eric Chaney of Morgan Stanley.
The activity has been due to a rush by French investors to profit from tax breaks by investing in life insurance policies.
"Insurance companies collect a lot of money at the end of the year. The first six weeks of the year are traditionally when you have a lot of cash in the market," he said.
He did not see big losses at the 10-year end but said there could be a major correction in the intermediate part of the yield curve.

Lindsay said two-to-three year BTAN maturities were expensive with the money market BTAN curve too flat compared with history and the German curve. Longer term, the seven-year maturity point was looking dear after recent outperformance.
He said current yield levels could spark re-appraisal by investors of their asset allocations that could weigh on the bond market and saw equities as the most likely beneficiary.
He said domestic investors' appetite to seek yield elsewhere was also steering interest into the deutschemark block with Dutch government debt looking attractive.
He noted domestic bond-based investment vehicles and life insurers have significant room to invest outside the French market as they are significantly below limits permitted by law.
